newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Salman Rushdie urges economic pressure on Iran.
newsitem.headline: Salman Rushdie urges economic pressure on Iran.

text.p: British author Salman Rushdie called on Monday for European countries to ostracise Iran for refusing to withdraw a seven-year-old death edict against him.

The controversial author, in Vienna for one night to perform a live reading from his latest book "The Moor's Last Sigh", met Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky and discussed ways to step up pressure on Iran.

"I think there have to be economic measures certainly and it has to be shown to the Iranians that they will suffer if they continue to threaten the lives of European citizens", he told reporters on a clandestine visit.

Indian-born Rushdie has lived in hiding and with permanent protection since 1989, when Iranian revolutionary leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini issued a death threat, or "fatwa", against him for his novel "The Satanic Verses".
The book was denounced as blasphemy against Islam.
Iran says it is powerless to lift the fatwa, which can only be revoked by the man who issued it, but Khomeini died in 1989.
The European Union has made headway on blunting the fatwa since France launched a diplomatic initiative almost two years ago when it held the EU's rotating presidency.
But the critical dialogue had not gone far enough according to Rushdie.
"The EU, although it has been very determined orally to get agreements, has put very few teeth into that process", he said. "The Iranians will change when they are made to change."
During their meeting, the Austrian chancellor had promised to push for further action when he next spoke to the current Irish presidency, Rushdie said.
"(Our meeting) is another statement by an EU leader of the importance of defending these principles," he said.
Asked if he regretted publishing the contentious book, Rushdie said: "To regret it would be to regret five years of my life, and I am extremely pleased with 'The Satanic Verses'."
It had been essential to continue his work as a writer and attend readings and book signings.
"I think it would be absurd and a defeat to wait for permission from some kind of despot in the Middle East to tell you if you can do things," he said.

Rushdie, who was awarded Austria's state prize for European literature in 1994, praised the literary openness of the country. He will perform the reading on Tuesday night at Vienna's historic theatre, the Burgtheater.
